Apprendre du passé, créer le futur : un: Learning from the past, creating the future: a living-memory workshop in Montréal-Nord
Découvrez Le passé reste vivant, un atel: Discover Le passé reste vivant, a workshop that is redefining third places in Montréal-Nord and giving the neighbourhood’s young people a chance to express themselves.
Niti Marcelle Mueth, co-fondatrice de l': Niti Marcelle Mueth, co-founder of the community organization Learning Loop. Photo credit: Gaëlle Leroyer
Dans l’imaginaire collectif, Montréal-No: In the collective imagination, Montréal-Nord too often evokes the same images: violence, poverty, marginalization. We forget that this territory carries something else too. It is a place where generations have developed a culture of solidarity and engagement. Many community organizations, artists, educators and activists build concrete alternatives there, day after day. They do so drawing on a memory marked by the wounds of the past.
Montréal-Nord porte les traces d’événeme: Montréal-Nord bears the traces of landmark events that have deeply shaped its history and collective identity. This memory is marked, among other things, by the death of Fredy Villanueva in 2008. The young man, killed by police in Parc Henri-Bourassa, became a symbol: that of a neighbourhood in anger, of a community in search of justice.
Aujourd’hui encore, alors que l’arrondis: Even today, as the borough bears the marks of deindustrialization and urban marginalization, local initiatives are seeking to revive a broader memory. It is in this context that the interactive workshop Le passé reste vivant, led by Hoodstock and Learning Loop and running throughout the summer, is emerging. I had the chance to meet one of Learning Loop’s co-founders to understand the importance of this initiative and the mission of her community organization.
<strong>C’est au café St-Henri dans le q: It is at Café St-Henri in the Villeray neighbourhood that we meet Niti Marcelle Mueth, co-founder of the community organization Learning Loop, to talk about Montréal-Nord and the initiative Le passé reste vivant. This series of three workshops begins this Saturday, July 12, and will be followed by two more sessions this summer.
La playlist du café diffuse des airs d’A: The café’s playlist is playing Latin American tunes. Celia Cruz’s La vida es un carnaval rises from the speakers like a manifesto in music: despite hardship, joy remains an act of resistance. Though she has a soft voice and laughing eyes, her tone is firm. Niti talks to us about heritage, transmission, wounds that need healing.
Dans moins de 48 heures, elle co-animera: In less than 48 hours, she will co-host the first of the interactive workshops for youth in Montréal-Nord, a neighbourhood too often reduced to its stereotypes: violence, poverty, marginalization. But Montréal-Nord, Niti insists, is not just that for the people and the young people who live there. And she rejects simplistic generalizations. “Realities are many, and so are the stories,” she says. “We tend to talk about working-class neighbourhoods as a homogeneous bloc. But no.”
C’est cette image figée que Niti veut qu: This is the fixed image Niti wants to question. When the reputation attached to Montréal-Nord comes up, she hides neither her irritation nor her lucidity. For her, the real problem is the representations people have of it. “Everything that comes from the outside is a perception. Those people don’t know what it’s like to live there. Yet so many positive things are happening there.”
« Montréal-Nord, c’est un des quartiers: “Montréal-Nord is one of the most underserved neighbourhoods when it comes to cultural activities. It’s also a neighbourhood that’s fairly far from downtown Montréal. There’s really a need to offer young people opportunities they might not find as much as youth who live closer to the centre. It lets us give them autonomy, but also let them know they have the possibility to do whatever they want in life.”
Celle qui est artiste visuelle et médiat: The visual artist and cultural mediator takes a clear stance in the activities she supervises. She refuses to judge young people or to try to “correct” them. “Even though I’ve spent time with young people in precarious situations, on the street or using drugs, my role isn’t to change their lives or to tell them ‘what you’re doing is wrong.’ In the end, they do what they have to do to survive.” And through these workshops, she wants to give them hope, as well as the feeling of being seen and understood.
Niti a grandi entre Ahunstic et Pierrefo: Niti grew up between Ahuntsic and Pierrefonds, neighbourhoods whose stories aren’t necessarily alike, even if they share certain struggles. This dual experience feeds her conviction: talking about working-class neighbourhoods isn’t telling a single, homogeneous story, but a mosaic of paths and realities. She stresses this diversity to avoid reducing young people to a fixed image or a single destiny.
<strong>Trois temps pour partager l’hist: Three moments to share history and compose the future
Les ateliers proposés lors de l’initiati: The workshops offered as part of the Le passé reste vivant initiative form a temporal trilogy conceived by Learning Loop to explore Black memory through the past, the present and the future.
Affiche de l'initiative Le passé reste v: Poster for the Le passé reste vivant initiative, starting July 12, 2025. Photo credit: Gaëlle Leroyer
Le premier volet sera consacré à l’histo: The first part will focus on the history of Black communities in Quebec, Montréal and Canada. “We mostly talk about Black history so that young people understand how and why they are here,” Niti explains. The goal is to open the door to these often forgotten or seldom-told stories, so that young people can situate themselves within a living collective memory.
Le deuxième volet, qui aura lieu le 19 j: The second part, on July 19, will offer an overview of the present. “We’ll talk about how [young people] feel today in society,” Niti explains, “based on what they understood from the workshop on the past and how they feel it affects their present.” This session will address the question of “how do we assert our identities and our collective power in a system that seeks to divide us?”, according to the event description. Niti insists that these young people must not be constantly forced to deconstruct stereotyped images imposed on them: “It’s not necessarily Black people’s responsibility to break this image that we didn’t give ourselves. It’s more about recognizing our worth and knowing that we do what we need to do, but not with the goal of proving something.” The aim here is above all to give young people a space to reflect, share and equip themselves to better take back power over their collective narrative.
Enfin, le dernier volet consacré au futu: Finally, the last part, devoted to the future, invites young people to imagine possible and desirable futures, an exercise that also makes room for Afrofuturism. This vision, which blends Black culture, science fiction and radical hope, proposes rethinking the future by valuing the creativity, innovation and resilience of Black communities. The idea: “to imagine futures in which we thrive, in which we are free to do what we want.” It is about projecting oneself forward to dream of worlds where emancipation and social justice are central. As Niti puts it, “It’s up to us to assert ourselves and recognize what we want.” This last workshop then acts as a catalyst, a place where new ways of being, creating and acting are invented.
La finalité des ateliers est de créer de: The aim of the workshops is to create collective or individual works whose final form has yet to be defined. They will take shape as things go along. This deliberate vagueness reflects an essential freedom: that of letting emerge what needs to emerge, without preset constraints. What matters most is that these voices take their place, that they are carried, seen, heard and felt, Niti explains. It is a space of authentic expression where young people can take ownership of their narrative, unfiltered.
« Souvent, quand je travaille avec les j: “Often, when I work with young people, what they tell me is that adults really don’t take them seriously, or that they aren’t heard. Their voice matters, just as much as anyone else’s.”
<strong>Learning Loop : un tiers-lieu gr: Learning Loop: a free third place to create, learn and reconnect
Learning Loop mise sur l’éducation popul: Learning Loop relies on popular and collaborative education as an engine of change. The community organization is first and foremost the story of two sisters: Niti Marcelle Mueth and Taïna Mueth. One studied community health and psychiatry, the other art therapy and graphic design. Together, in 2022, they co-founded a unique space, conceived as a free “third place,” where immigrant and marginalized communities can create, learn and build connections in different ways. “Our goal was really just to give people opportunities and to have a place where they can not only connect, but learn, share knowledge, create for free.”
Learning Loop was born out of a glaring gap. “There was really that gap in Montréal. (…) Lots of places to gather cost money or aren’t made for connecting with your community,” Niti explains. The two sisters, who grew up between Ahuntsic and Pierrefonds, remember a childhood marked by the absence of community spaces. “Apart from school and home, there really wasn’t anywhere. We grew up in church, so we had a community there, but outside of that… we had no contact with Quebec society.”
Ce besoin d’appartenance et d’expression: This need for belonging and free expression led to the creation of monthly pay-what-you-can workshops. Places that could be “refuges” where you come without having to consume, “just to talk, create, connect.” Because for her, art isn’t a hobby but a necessity. “Art kept me alive. It’s what allowed me to stay grounded. (…) Even if it’s not art, having something that grounds them a little really helps.”
Dans ces ateliers, l’art devient un outi: In these workshops, art becomes a therapeutic tool, a way to break silences. “It’s a way to heal, to express yourself, but it’s also a way of getting messages across, of being understood. Art has a lot of uses other than just being beautiful.”
Pour la jeune femme d’origine haïtienne: For the young woman of Haitian and Cameroonian origin, this approach makes even more sense in racialized communities where mental health issues remain underrepresented. “Especially in our community, because everything to do with therapy, psychology, is still a bit taboo. I think it’s less and less the case, fortunately. But with the experiences we’ve had, the intergenerational trauma, there’s so much to heal.”
Elle voit d’ailleurs dans la pratique de: She also sees in the practice of art therapy a kind of catharsis. “As long as we don’t do the healing work, it keeps happening. People have health problems or mental health problems and they don’t even know where it comes from.”
Depuis deux ans, les deux fondatrices po: For two years, the two founders have carried this project on a volunteer basis. “It’s a passion project. We don’t make money doing this. We do it because we believe in the impact it can have on a young person’s life.” Niti knows something about that. “I’ve seen how much art can change lives. That’s what it did for me. That’s what I want to offer young people too.” For her, art makes it possible to open breaches. She speaks of an art that heals, that offers a language for what can’t always be said. It’s what allowed me to stay grounded.”
« Ma mère n'était pas très heureuse à l': “My mother wasn’t very happy with the idea that I’d be an artist or that I’d study in more artistic fields. I really fought for what I believed in. Today, I’m happy to be able to show young people that it’s possible. That’s what not limiting yourself means.”
Pour Niti, ce n’est pas forcément l’art: For Niti, it’s not necessarily art that matters, but having something to hold on to. A space, an activity, a place of reference points. Something concrete in the world that gives meaning, value, a sense of autonomy and confidence. “Even if it’s not art, having something that grounds them a little. It really helps,” she says, grateful to have witnessed that power.
À travers Learning Loop et d’autres acte: Through Learning Loop and other community actors like Hoodstock, another idea of Montréal-Nord is taking shape: a place where solidarity, creativity and collective memory nourish possible futures. Beyond the stereotypes, these initiatives remind us that the future of Montréal-Nord is already being written today, in the solidarity, memory and creativity of its youth.
